To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the development of autoimmune diabetes in the NOD mouse is regulated by T cells that are present in nondiabetic NBD mice, that are CD4+ and that depend on thymic activity for their function.
the presence of suppressor CD4+ T lymphocytes, which depend on thymic function for their development, delays the onset of diabetes mellitus in NOD mice.
suppressor phenomena are detectable in the NOD model of autoimmune diabetes and that these phenomena may be mediated by CD4+ T cell subsets that are dependent on an intact thymus for function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new model for insulin-dependent (Type 1) diabetes mellitus.
the role of T lymphocytes in the development of autoimmune diabetes.
the development of antithyroid, antireproductive, and antipancreas autoimmunity in NOD mice, and with the role of suppressor T cells in the pathogenesis of these autoimmune diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results presented in the manuscript support the hypothesis that regulatory CD4 T cells play a role in the prevention of diabetes in NOD female mice.
T cells from nondiabetics NOD mice can inhibit diabetes development in recipients.
T suppressor cells are present in nondiabetic mice, but that their activity is not sufficient to prevent diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thymus is a source of suppressor T cells which delay the onset of spontaneous diabetes in the NOD model.
the NOD mice have a defective immune regulatory mechanism.
we have shown that T cells can be induced to suppress diabetes transfer in the nonobese diabetic mouse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thymus plays a role in the development of diabetes.
T cell-mediated suppression is a major factor in preventing the onset of diabetes.
the NOD mouse is a good model to study the development of diabetes.
